title: Checkout service and pricing rules
idea: The core design is one CheckoutService that reprices the cart, reserves stock and charges payment, talking to each part only through an interface.

analogy.text: A supermarket till. The cashier scans every item at today's price, applies the coupons in order, checks the shelf count, then runs the card.
analogy.breaks: A cashier can bend a coupon rule; a PricingRule cannot.

points: CheckoutService is a facade: callers see one `checkout` method, nothing else.
Each discount is a `PricingRule` strategy; new promotions are new classes.
Rules run in list order, and each one sees the running total.
Stock is reserved for all lines or none, and released if payment fails.

steps.caption: U-7 checks out a cart with three mugs and one T-shirt.
The service reprices every line from the catalog, not from the cart.
Each PricingRule takes its discount from the running total, in list order.
Inventory checks every line first, then reserves them all together.
The gateway charges the discounted total once.
Success returns an Order with subtotal, discount and total frozen.
U-9 wants the T-shirt, but none are left. Nothing is reserved or charged.
U-8's card is declined. The service releases the mugs it had reserved.

code.title: Service and interfaces
code.caption: The core flow with every collaborator injected. This trimmed version charges inside checkout; page 4 splits out the PENDING_PAYMENT step. CartItem drops the price here; Line holds the catalog price used at checkout.

walk.text: Wire the service: catalog prices, stock, one pricing rule and a fake gateway.
U-7 buys three mugs and a T-shirt; print the frozen totals.
U-9 hits empty stock; U-8 is declined. Then count the mugs left.
Two interfaces are the swap points: pricing rules and the payment gateway.
Reserve checks every line before changing any; release gives units back.
Reprice from the catalog, then let each rule cut the running total.
Reserve, charge, release on decline, and return an immutable Order.

code.title: A new rule, rule order
code.caption: A buy-3-pay-for-2 rule added as a new class; no old class is edited. The same cart priced with three rule lists.

walk.text: One cart and two rules: 10 percent off above 2000.00, and 3 mugs for 2.
Price the cart with one rule, then with both rules in each order.
The same loop as the service: each rule cuts the running total.
The new strategy only needs a SKU and the buy and pay counts.
Every full group of three makes one unit free; never discount below zero.

pitfalls: Do not add `if (saleDay)` branches to CheckoutService; add a PricingRule class instead.
Never trust the price stored in the cart; reprice from the catalog at checkout.
Rule order changes the total; make the order explicit configuration, not list luck.

quiz.q: What does RuleOrder print on its last line?
quiz.why: 10 percent of 229600 leaves 206640. The mug rule then removes one free mug, 49900, giving 156740.

takeaway: One facade service; every promotion is a PricingRule applied in a stated order.

starters: Is a list of PricingRules the chain of responsibility pattern?
How do I stop two promotions from stacking when they should not?
Where should the rule order come from in production?
